title: Willey video release sought
article: A clash between police, the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs, the B.C. Civil Liberties Association and the family of Clayton Willey over a surveillance video shot at the Prince George RCMP detachment has reignited controversy over the notorious Taser case.

It's been five years since a coroner's inquest ruled that the 33-year-old Willey died of a cocaine overdose in 2003, despite his family's insistence that excessive force on the part of arresting RCMP officers contributed to his death. During the trial, jurors reviewed, among other evidence, footage from RCMP video cameras showing Willey dragged down a hallway by an RCMP officer, apparently Tasered in an elevator, and then shocked by the energy weapon in a booking area at least twice more. Willey was later taken to hospital and died of a heart attack.

Now one of the province's leading aboriginal groups and a civil liberties' organization wants the RCMP to release the surveillance tape, in the hopes that public outrage will trigger greater police accountability, said David Eby, executive director of the BCCLA.

"It's very disturbing footage to watch, very similar to the Dziekanski tape in its emotional impact," said Eby, referring to the footage of the death of Polish passenger Robert Dziekanski in Vancouver Airport in 2007. "If it's possible, it's almost worse."

Grand Chief Stewart Phillip, president of the UBCIC, said the video left him 'deeply concerned' and reflected what he described as a nationwide problem of aboriginal men dying in the hands of the police.

The groups claim the version they watched -- after a Vancouver-based freelance journalist submitted a freedom of information request -- shows: an RCMP SUV arriving in the detachment garage; Willey being dragged down a hallway, hog-tied, with his hands bound behind his back and tethered to his feet; Willey's head hitting a elevator; a Taser targeting Willey's back; Willey being dragged out of an elevator, into a booking area, where he's Tasered at least twice more.

Eby says he wants to see a tape with no date or time codes -- and both he and Willey's family said there are missing incidents in the one screened recently, particularly a moment when Willey is dragged from the SUV by a 'hobble' -- the rope of the hog tie -- and his head hits a part of the vehicle and then the garage floor.
Eby saw a version of the tape after the FOI request this year; the Willey family viewed another version of tape before the coroner's inquest in 2004.

However, Sgt. Tim Shields, who's seen both versions, said, "I don't know how they could see that" and insisted nothing radical was removed from the tape shown to Eby. "The video was submitted first to Crown counsel, then the coroner's inquest, where 100 per cent of the video involving Mr. Willey was submitted. It was edited so approximately eight separate camera views could be seen in sequence on one video tape."
The reason, said Shields, that the point where Willey was bounced from the SUV is not on video is the detachment's system at the time rotated among the building's cameras.

"The camera system recorded approximately two dozen cameras onto a VHS videotape," he said. "The system would automatically rotate the camera views that were being saved on the tape. The system was not capable of recording all 24 views at the same time."

Shields said the police have not been approached by the Willey family about releasing the tape but the RCMP did receive a request from a documentary filmmaker, which was denied. He added there is an "invitation" out to the Willeys to again view the full tape, if they wish, as well as all the evidence related to the coroner's inquest.
